deep.reconstruction: The page has two parts. (a) The upper two thirds is a heavily struck-through pencil draft of a letter beginning 'Lieber Vater!'. The legible surviving text says that when he wrote at Easter that he would like to stay until Pfingsten (Whitsun) in [a place, unclear; transcription reads 'Akademie' but this is doubtful], he had intended to work there for the Colloquium, and that he could not get finished here. He says he had proposed a topic and, since his Vortrag (talk) was ready, hoped the elaboration would not take much effort. Much of the text is crossed out or illegible; the letter is personal and not mathematical. (b) The lower part, starting at 'I Mit Einschluss der Ausnahmefaelle', is a counting of conditions for a polyhedron, apparently to decide how many conditions of a 'second class' remain when polyhedra are specified by their angles. Data in the case marked I: total number of angles = 25 (reading uncertain), conditions of the first class = 7+p, conditions 'elements' = 2(p-2), hence conditions of the second class = 7 (the '7+' is underlined and the result 7 is written beside it). Then: z = 63, f = 36, p = 29, conditions of the second class 7. Case II: taking some points as edge points (Kantenpunkte, reading unclear), total number of angles = 23 (reading uncertain). The verso/next page (bound with it in the transcription, not this scan) works the same numbers: with s = 63 edges, p = 29 points, f = 36 faces, 2s = 126 is the number of face angles; 2s - p - f - 2(p-2) = 126 - 29 - 36 - 54 = 7; and 'first class' conditions f + c = 90 (c = 54 = 2(p-2)), 126 - 90 = 36, 36 - 29 = 7. My reading (marked as mine, not certain): z/s = number of edges, p = vertices, f = faces; the numbers satisfy Euler's relation p - z + f = 29 - 63 + 36 = 2, so the object is a convex-type polyhedron of genus 0. The count appears to be a dimension count: 126 face angles minus relations among them (one angle-sum relation per face, plus 2(p-2) relations, perhaps spherical-link conditions at the vertices) minus p leaves 7 free 'second class' conditions. What problem this serves (e.g. determining a polyhedron from its angles, or a Colloquium topic) is unclear from the page.
errors: The counts p=29, z=63, f=36 satisfy Euler's formula, so no arithmetic error was found in the legible numbers.
The identification of 'z', 's', 'p', 'f', 'c', 'a' as edges, vertices, faces, etc. is my inference, not stated on the page.
The legibility of 'Gesammtzahl Winkel = 25' and '= 23' is poor; the meaning of these totals is not established.
The reason for subtracting p (and the meaning of 'first/second class' conditions) is not recoverable from this page, so correctness of the method cannot be judged.
